on_calabogie_bouldering.blurb: Calabogie is a bouldering area in the forest of eastern Ontario, about 100 km west of Ottawa. The stone is hard, clean and fairly compact, and the boulders are modest in size with flat landings, which makes it a friendly place to learn to boulder as well as to push limits. Most problems fall between V0 and V6, with a handful of harder ones beyond that, and the climbing leans toward fingery, powerful movement and friction on the harder lines. The area is lightly visited compared with Canada's biggest bouldering venues. Bring a pad and watch for poison ivy near the cliff base and along the trails.
on_calabogie_bouldering.parking_note: A signed lot sits on Calabogie Road (County Road 508), a couple of kilometres beyond the turn for Barrett Chute. It is the starting point for the main boulders and the cliff-line boulders. Use the lot rather than the road shoulder.
on_calabogie_bouldering.approach: Several marked trails climb from the lot to the boulders and cliff. Expect roughly a quarter to half an hour of easy hiking depending on the zone; one trail avoids the swampy stretch.

on_buffalo_crag.blurb: Buffalo Crag is a quiet stretch of escarpment cliff in the Rattlesnake Point conservation area near Milton, west of Toronto. It is mainly a traditional and top-rope venue, with cracks, ledges and some slightly overhanging sections, and the bolts at the tops of the climbs are anchors for top-roping rather than lower-offs, so plan to rig from above. Grades run from very easy to hard, but the bulk sit between 5.5 and 5.10, which suits newer trad leaders and groups. It tends to be calmer than the neighbouring main cliff on weekends. Dry weather from spring through fall is best because wet rock turns slick; bring a standard rack, a helmet, and plenty of cordelette for the set-back anchors.
on_buffalo_crag.parking_note: Use the parking at the Rattlesnake Point conservation area near Milton and walk from there.
on_buffalo_crag.approach: Marked trails lead along the escarpment from the main climbing area at Rattlesnake Point to the crag, a walk of around a quarter of an hour.

or_spring_mountain_climbs.blurb: Spring Mountain is a remote cliff in the Blue Mountains of northeast Oregon, high in the national forest between La Grande and Pendleton at around 4,500 feet. A long wall of andesite, close kin to basalt, it offers technical crimps, juggy ledges, bulges and steep overhangs, with some cracks and a few slabby faces. Bolted sport lines outnumber trad, and the wall is only about a hundred feet tall, so the climbs are single pitch. Most routes fall between 5.8 and 5.11, with a few harder and a few easy ones. The elevation means snow lingers, so late spring through early fall is the usual window. Expect a long gravel drive and a quiet crag.
or_spring_mountain_climbs.parking_note: From Interstate 84 take exit 243 and follow Summit Road north, then continue on gravel forest roads for about eight to nine miles. Follow signs and branch roads to a turnaround blocked by large boulders near the trail start.
or_spring_mountain_climbs.approach: A short trail from the road end reaches the base of the wall.

or_main_wall_the.blurb: The Main Wall is the headline cliff at Trout Creek, a canyon on the Deschutes River in central Oregon. It is a long row of basalt columns split by vertical cracks, corners and stem boxes, and every route here is traditional. The rock is rough and grippy, so bring tape and a generous rack of cams. Most lines sit between 5.10 and 5.12, with a few easier and a few harder, and the climbing is sustained crack work without much rest. The wall faces west, so it gets afternoon sun and shade earlier in the day. Getting to it involves some exposed boulder-hopping and scrambling, which may not suit everyone. The mesa above is private property.
or_main_wall_the.parking_note: Drive to the Trout Creek recreation area at the Deschutes River, signed from the town of Gateway north of Madras, and park at the day-use area beside the campground. The final miles are on dirt road that ordinary cars manage.
or_main_wall_the.approach: Follow the old road upstream along the river from the day-use area, then take one of the trails up to the base. The Main Wall requires exposed boulder-hopping and some third and fourth class scrambling.

or_mill_creek_falls.blurb: Mill Creek Falls is a scattering of boulders in the Rogue River country near Prospect, in southwest Oregon, close to the waterfalls and the trail that winds among the river's giant boulders. The problems are bunched tightly together, with only a few minutes of walking from one to the next, and cover a wide range from V0 up to the double digits, with the heaviest concentration in the V1 to V5 range. The area has had little traffic in recent years, so expect moss and some rough landings; brushes and extra pads help. The surrounding forest keeps things damp and green, so choose a dry spell.
or_mill_creek_falls.parking_note: From Medford head north on Oregon 62 through Shady Cove and Trail and over the large bridge. Follow the Mill Creek Falls sign on the right, take the next right and a short road to the lot.
or_mill_creek_falls.approach: Walk down the trail on the left side of the lot and stay left to reach the boulders.

or_west.blurb: West is the bouldering zone on the west side of Cline Falls, a compact riverside basalt area on the Deschutes a few miles outside Redmond in central Oregon. The problems here are mostly short and approachable, with the large majority between V0 and V4, plus a few harder lines and a handful of roped climbs. The riverside setting is popular with swimmers and picnickers in summer, so expect company on hot days. The nearby cliff stays shaded until mid afternoon in summer, and the river runs higher in fall and winter, which affects how you reach some of the boulders.
or_west.parking_note: Park in the large pullout off Highway 126 about four miles west of Redmond, across from the entrance to the state scenic viewpoint.
or_west.approach: Take the trail downhill from the pullout and follow the river downstream to the falls. A gully through the cliff downstream of the falls gives easier access to the boulders, especially when the river is high.

or_christian_brothers_east_side.blurb: The east side of the Christian Brothers is the busiest part of a cluster of towers at Smith Rock, tucked just beyond the Dihedrals and below Asterisk Pass. The rock is similar to the neighbouring walls, and the climbing is mostly single pitch around the base of the towers, with sport lines outnumbering trad by a wide margin. The majority of routes fall between 5.10 and 5.13, with a small number of easier lines and a few of the park's hardest. Expect fingery faces and cracks, a steady crowd on good weekends, and heat in summer; spring and fall are the comfortable seasons.
or_christian_brothers_east_side.parking_note: Use the main day-use lot by the welcome center, then walk across the footbridge to the river trail.
or_christian_brothers_east_side.approach: After the footbridge turn left on the River Trail and follow it for about a quarter mile, passing the Dihedrals to reach the base of the towers just before Asterisk Pass.

or_bat_wall.blurb: Bat Wall is one of the main sections of Broughton Bluff, a cluster of basalt cliffs at the mouth of the Columbia Gorge, within easy reach of Portland. It is a sport wall known for steeper, harder climbing, with nearly all routes bolted and grades concentrated between 5.10 and 5.13. Winter tends to be damp, so late spring through fall is the more dependable time. Poison oak grows around the base and trails, so watch your footing and clothing. Sunny weekends bring a crowd.
or_bat_wall.parking_note: Heading east on Interstate 84, leave at the exit for Lewis and Clark State Park, go left at the junction, continue under the railroad bridge and pull into the lot on your left.
or_bat_wall.approach: A trail climbs the hillside from the lot to the cliffs, a walk of roughly 10 to 25 minutes depending on which wall you are heading for.
